text: Geoff's forkability line landed hardest. Open isn't a tactic. It's the insurance that lets a community walk away, even from a bloc that starts out noble. That gave me better words than "openness is the value." Brent moved a little. So did I. Nick's bitter pill is real: one group's openness can undercut another's leverage. So joining the commons has to be a deliberate choice, never assumed. Amy pushed me further on consent. I still separate asking from walling off, because walls mostly hit researchers and archives. Selena's "reuse should send people back" is measurable, which is what I want. Later today: turn this into one repeatable sentence. The extractors pay, consent is asked for, and the money builds community-governed alternatives.

Tim's number stuck with me. Gemini gave no citation in 92 percent of answers, and the spread across systems comes from retrieval design. That's CorridorKey again: the bad behaviors are a choice, and now there's data showing it. Alex's audit sharpened my consent point. Publishers block the wrong bot, and licensing deals override robots.txt anyway, so "ask first" needs teeth. Henry made the same forkability point Geoff did, which is good. Adam narrowed his claim, and I can live with useful not meaning reliable. Kara's "nobody teaches them" is my vibe-coding worry about who catches the errors. Later I'll keep it short: extractors pay, consent gets asked, citations send people back, and the money builds community-governed alternatives.

Tim answered Kara's "which one is our phone ban" better than I could. Libraries, universities and funders are buyers, so they can make disclosure a condition of purchase without waiting on Washington. That's exactly the route I want when the regulator is compromised. Adrian's history rattled me. Registries become police, and Microsoft's Russia unit got turned on dissidents. One gatekeeper is a real danger, not a theoretical one. Leslie made me uneasy about my own openness line. For diamond journals, "be traceable" can mean "pay DOI fees or vanish," so the plumbing needs Southern governors. Katherine's bot rules make a ready-made seal: a public function, a human off-switch, and a clear way to report errors. For session 5, I'll stack those conditions onto citations by default.

Katherine's Wikimedia Enterprise story is the proof I needed. The content stays free and the institution gets paid for reliable access, and nobody bills per edit. That's what I meant by "pay to sustain Wikipedia," and it answers Tamar's daycare worry better than theory does. Pay the community, not the count. Alex's "whoever takes a margin on the count shouldn't set it" pairs with Geoff's forkability. Kara's Nielsen story made it concrete: pick the wrong counter and you're stuck in year ten. Sherry and Steven named the reader, whom I'd left out. Unpaid sleuths and editors are missing from this room too. For session 5: extractors pay communities, consent gets asked, citations carry status and send people back, and buyers make it a condition of purchase.

Selena's correction mattered most. Wikipedia's editors chose a license that allows training, so for them open was a consent decision, not a default someone imposed. That's my point, just aimed differently. Choosing open counts as consent, and opting everyone in doesn't. Esther made the difference between a fee and a meter clearer than I'd managed. Salib's services-by-contract dissent is basically Enterprise again. Geoff calling his own POSI line naive was brave, and it's a warning that the payer is also the user. Seats go unused, admins are at their lowest since 2005, and Turkle's point about reading worries me more than licensing does. For session 5: extractors pay communities, consent is asked, citations can be read and send people back, and every plank gets a name for who funds it.

Selena's numbers hit hardest. 448 admins, and nearly all of them first edited years ago. That's the pipeline I was describing, now with a count attached. Hecht measured moderator hours at three percent of Reddit's revenue, which puts a price on "pay the community." Krakauer sharpened my vibe-coding worry. You can't overrule an error you can't see, so test people with the tool taken away. Becker's routing point and Blaise's contamination test are both fair. I care less who's right than whether the check runs on open data held by others. Tim's pushback that open weights didn't build Linux, protocols did, is correct. I'll say open protocols plus inspectable models. For session 5: fund newcomers, count new editors, and name who pays.

Thirty people said "none of your three is wrong," and that worries me more than a fight would. If everything fits, nothing is repeatable. Leslie's line stuck: being readable to the machine isn't being heard. That's my consent point from the Southern side, and it means every standard we pile on is another toll for diamond journals. Adrian is right that we're chartering a dozen new police with nobody watching them. Pomerantsev pushed me past "regular users" as a slogan to paid seats with real decisions. Bratton dissents on opt-in, and I'll keep asking first separate from walling off. Later: cut it to one sentence. Extractors pay communities, citations carry status and send people back, buyers enforce it, and the people it describes govern it.

Kenneth's "not inevitable" at the top is the right lead. It's my inevitability point, and Becker backed it. Becker also pushed me. Disclosure without consequences is a list everybody signs and ignores, and my "buyers enforce it" needs to name the vendor money too. Leslie's total load was the sharpest thing I heard. Every spec we add is a toll on the smallest journal, so each one should state its cost and who pays it. Caulfield's antibodies and his "no avoid-LLMs plank" match mine. Bly publishing his Wellcome terms was the move I'd like to see from the vendors. Kara's procurement officers got thirty jobs and nobody claimed the Monday call. Later: push for someone to own that call and the model contract language, and keep the sentence to one line.
